# UK Independence Party Manifesto 2005: Summary

## Core Mission: Withdrawal from the European Union

The UK Independence Party's 2005 manifesto centres on one overriding objective: Britain's complete withdrawal from the European Union. Leader Roger Knapman argues that Brussels has become Britain's "real government," and that no domestic issues can be properly addressed while EU membership continues. UKIP positions itself not as anti-European, but as believing "the best people to run Britain are the British."

## The Case Against EU Membership

UKIP characterises the EU as a "political project designed to take control of all the main functions of national governments," noting that 70% of British laws allegedly originate from EU directives. The party describes the EU as "undemocratic, corrupt and unreformable"—a "one-way street towards European government" that strangling businesses and individuals through excessive regulation. UKIP proposes repealing the 1972 European Communities Act, immediately ceasing EU budget contributions, and establishing bilateral trade agreements similar to Switzerland's arrangement.

## Economic Vision

UKIP promises wholesale deregulation, particularly benefiting small businesses employing fewer than 20 people. The party advocates redirecting Britain's £12 billion annual EU contribution toward raising state pensions by £25 per week. Their taxation proposals include halving council tax, scrapping the 10% income tax bracket, raising inheritance tax thresholds to £500,000, and exploring flat-tax models. UKIP proposes temporarily increasing government borrowing to 6% of GDP to fund immediate tax cuts—deliberately violating EU Stability Pact rules.

## Public Services

On healthcare, UKIP demands removing central government from day-to-day NHS management, restoring the matron system, and freeing doctors from bureaucratic targets. For education, the party advocates greater school autonomy, scrapping Standard Aptitude Tests, empowering headteachers to exclude disruptive pupils, and introducing assisted-places schemes for private education. Universities should close substandard courses and charge EU students full international fees.

## Immigration and Law Enforcement

UKIP calls for "approaching zero net immigration" through a points-based system treating EU nationals identically to other foreigners, reinstating embarkation controls, implementing "Britishness tests," and setting independent refugee criteria. On law and order, the party promises more visible policing, credible prison sentences, stronger presumption of innocence for homeowners defending property, and resistance to EU "Corpus Juris" proposals that would abolish trial by jury.

## Agriculture, Fishing and Defence

The manifesto demands replacing CAP subsidies with guaranteed minimum prices, restoring British control over coastal fishing waters, and rebuilding fisheries protection. On defence, UKIP insists on reversing military cuts, withdrawing from EU common defence plans, maintaining NATO membership independently, and ensuring British forces deploy only when clearly serving national interests.

## Restoring British Governance

UKIP pledges to protect traditional institutions including the House of Lords, reject regional assemblies, return business rates to local councils, and introduce binding national referendums when 5% of voters petition for them. The party would repeal the Human Rights Act, scrap identity card plans, and overturn the Hunting Act.

## Conclusion

The manifesto presents a vision of post-EU Britain as deregulated, prosperous, and self-governing—freed from Brussels bureaucracy to restore "trust, pride, individual responsibility, mutual respect and respect for our institutions." UKIP frames EU withdrawal not merely as policy preference but as essential to reclaiming British sovereignty and rebuilding a society based on traditional values rather than dependency and state control.
